CausalChain: Obesity/NAFLD → Elevated circulating FFAs → Reduced DGAT2 activity in HCC leads to less triglyceride synthesis → Accumulation of FFAs increases lipotoxic stress and dysregulates mitochondrial function & ESRRA–PROX1 axis → Activation of oncogenic signaling pathways (ER stress, inflammation) → Promotion of dedifferentiation, proliferation, and metastasis → Enhancement of DGAT2 restores triglyceride synthesis → Formation of protective lipid droplets → Sequestration of FFAs reduces lipotoxic and oncogenic stress → Decrease in tumor progression
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that in HCC, precise upregulation of DGAT2 activity—achieved through contemporary CRISPR activation systems or pharmacological inducers—will enhance triglyceride synthesis and promote the formation of lipid droplets that act as protective depots for sequestering lipotoxic FFAs. This sequestration not only alleviates direct lipotoxicity but also improves mitochondrial function and adjusts the ESRRA–PROX1 transcriptional network, thereby attenuating oncogenic signaling pathways such as ER stress and inflammatory responses. Leveraging technologies like single-cell transcriptomics and advanced lipidomic profiling will allow us to monitor these metabolic shifts and validate the therapeutic potential of DGAT2 enhancement in reducing tumor aggressiveness and improving patient outcomes.
Abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is often underpinned by metabolic dysregulation, particularly in contexts of obesity and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), which elevate circulating free fatty acids (FFAs). We propose that targeted enhancement of DGAT2 activity—using modern gene editing tools and small molecule activators—can rectify these metabolic imbalances by promoting the formation of protective triglyceride-rich lipid droplets. These droplets not only sequester lipotoxic FFAs but also restore mitochondrial function and modulate key transcriptional regulators (e.g., the ESRRA–PROX1 network). Collectively, this dual-action mechanism is hypothesized to dampen oncogenic signaling pathways such as ER stress and inflammatory cascades, thereby reducing tumor aggressiveness. Utilizing single-cell transcriptomics and advanced lipidomics, the proposed strategy offers a precise, patient-specific approach to validate and exploit this metabolic intervention, ultimately aiming to improve clinical outcomes in HCC patients.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis posited that enhancing DGAT2 in HCC would foster lipid droplet formation to sequester lipotoxic FFAs and reduce oncogenic signaling, improving outcomes. The revised hypothesis retains this core concept but expands on it by incorporating detailed mechanistic insights and modern technological approaches. Specifically, it now acknowledges additional established mechanisms (mitochondrial function and the ESRRA–PROX1 transcriptional axis) as part of the protective effect, explicitly cites the causal chain from metabolic dysregulation to tumor progression, and proposes the use of contemporary gene editing and multi-omics technologies to experimentally validate and refine the intervention in a patient-specific context.
